title: NGC 602 (Webb image)
caption: The young star cluster NGC 602, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 602 · constellation Hydrus · about 200000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, P. Zeidler, E. Sabbi, A. Nota, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Webb press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A star cluster sits within a big nebula of gas and dust in many colors. Dark ridges and peaks surround the cluster, lit on their inner sides, while layers of thin, see-through clouds drape over them. A huge number of distant galaxies show through the gas, along with a few much closer stars that appear large and bright.

This is NGC 602, a young star cluster near the edge of the Small Magellanic Cloud. That satellite galaxy is roughly 200 000 light-years from Earth. Its surroundings closely resemble conditions in the early Universe, with very small amounts of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium.

Dark clouds of dense dust and plenty of ionized gas suggest that stars are still forming here. That makes NGC 602 a valuable place to study star birth under conditions very different from those near the Sun. Webb combined its Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) and Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) to make the picture.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.03 x 2.45 arcminutes) and distance (200000 light years), the frame spans roughly 176 × 143 light-years. Its light set out about 200,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI recorded NGC 602 in near- and mid-infrared light. Blue shows 1.15 to 1.5 micrometers, cyan 2.1, green 2.77, yellow 3.35, orange 3.56 and red 4.8 and 10 micrometers.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colors are assigned to separate wavelengths rather than being what anyone would see.
